arXiv:2007.12049v2 [gr-qc] 07 Oct 2021

On holonomy singularities in general relativity & the Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility of spacetimes

Jan Sbierski ††thanks: Mathematical Institute, University of Oxford, Radcliffe Observatory Quarter, Woodstock Road, Oxford, OX2 6GG, United Kingdom
August 24, 2026
Abstract

This paper investigates the structure of gravitational singularities at the level of the connection. We show in particular that for FLRW spacetimes with particle horizons a local holonomy, which is related to a gravitational energy, becomes unbounded near the big-bang singularity. This implies the Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility of such FLRW spacetimes. Again using an unbounded local holonomy we also give a general theorem establishing the Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility of spherically symmetric weak null singularities which arise at the Cauchy horizon in the interior of black holes. Our theorem does not presuppose the mass-inflation scenario and in particular applies to the Reissner-Nordström-Vaidya spacetimes as well as to spacetimes which arise from small and generic spherically symmetric perturbations of two-ended subextremal Reissner-Nordström initial data for the Einstein-Maxwell-scalar field system. In [26], [27] Luk and Oh proved the C2C^{2}-formulation of strong cosmic censorship for this latter class of spacetimes – and based on their work we improve this to a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-formulation of strong cosmic censorship.

1 Introduction

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a smooth and time-oriented Lorentzian manifold. A Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension of (M,g)(M,g) is an isometric embedding ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} of MM into a Lorentzian manifold (M~,g~)(\tilde{M},\tilde{g}) of the same dimension, where g~\tilde{g} is a locally Lipschitz regular metric, such that ∂ι⁡(M)⊆M~\partial\iota(M)\subseteq\tilde{M} is non-empty. If no such Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension exists then we say that (M,g)(M,g) is Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible. Extensions of other regularities are defined analogously.

Our first main result is that cosmological warped product spacetimes with particle horizons are Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible. This class in particular contains the FLRW spacetimes with particle horizons.

∫1∞a⁡(t)a​(t)2+1​dt=∞.\displaystyle\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{a(t)}{\sqrt{a(t)^{2}+1}}\,dt=\infty\;.

Let M=(0,∞)×M¯M=(0,\infty)\times\overline{M} and consider the Lorentzian metric g=−d​t2+a​(t)2​g¯g=-dt^{2}+a(t)^{2}\,\overline{g} on MM. Then (M,g)(M,g) is Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible.

Our second main result is that spherically symmetric weak null singularities are Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible. A version of our results can be stated as follows:

Note that the spherically symmetric weak null singularities do admit future C0C^{0}-extensions!

1.1 Motivation

There are three main motivations for studying the low-regularity inextendibility of Lorentzian manifolds.

The first motivation comes from the expectation/possibility that if a solution to Einstein’s equations Rμ​ν−12​gμ​ν​R=2​Tμ​νR_{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}R=2T_{\mu\nu} can be continued as a weak solution, then classical time-evolution in general relativity continues, i.e., the classical theory does not break down. Here, it is of course crucial to discuss what we mean by a weak solution.

Considering for simplicity of discussion the vacuum Einstein equations Rμ​ν−12​gμ​ν​R=0R_{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}R=0, we see that they take the schematic form g​∂∂g+N⁡(g)​(∂g,∂g)=0g\partial\partial g+N(g)(\partial g,\partial g)=0, where N​(g)​(∂g,∂g)N(g)(\partial g,\partial g) is a nonlinearity that is quadratic in ∂g\partial g with coefficients depending on gg. If the metric is in C2C^{2} then clearly the strong, pointwise notion of a solution to Einstein’s equations is available. If only g∈C0g\in C^{0} and ∂g∈Lloc2\partial g\in L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}, then this regularity is still sufficient to define the classical notion of a weak solution, i.e., we require that for all smooth and compactly supported vector fields X,YX,Y on MM we have

(1.3) 0​=!​∫M(R⁡(X,Y)−12​g​(X,Y)⋅R)​volg=∫M(g​∂∂g+N⁡(g)​(∂g,∂g))​X​Y​−detg​d​x⏟=volg.0\overset{!}{=}\int_{M}\big(R(X,Y)-\frac{1}{2}g(X,Y)\cdot R\big)\mathrm{vol}_{g}=\int_{M}\big(g\partial\partial g+N(g)(\partial g,\partial g)\big)XY\underbrace{\sqrt{-\det g}\,dx}_{=\mathrm{vol}_{g}}\;.

After one integration by parts to move one of the derivatives from the term g​∂∂gg\partial\partial g over to the test fields X,YX,Y, we see that the regularity assumption g∈C0g\in C^{0} and ∂g∈Lloc2\partial g\in L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}} is sufficient to ensure that the coefficients of the test fields in (1.3) are in Lloc1L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}} – and thus the Einstein tensor Rμ​ν−12​gμ​ν​RR_{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}R is a well-defined distribution.

The regularity class g∈C0g\in C^{0} and ∂g∈Lloc2\partial g\in L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}} has been widely (e.g. [20], [16], [3], [2]) considered to be the largest regularity class that admits weak solutions in the above sense and still exhibits sufficient stability properties, cf. the approximation theorems in [16].11 1 In some references g∈C0g\in C^{0} is weakend to g,g−1∈Lloc∞g,g^{-1}\in L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}, cf. [16]. Although this seems reasonable from a PDE point of view, it clearly poses challenges for the physical interpretation and Lorentzian causality theory alike. Whether they can be overcome seems to be largely an open question. Let us also mention that the regularity class g∈C0g\in C^{0} and ∂g∈Lloc2\partial g\in L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}} is not necessary for the notion (1.3) of a weak solution: one can for example slightly widen it by only requiring that the products of Christoffel symbols which appear in the Einstein equations are locally integrable, [15], [16], but this has the disadvantage that one loses the good stability properties. Showing that a particular solution of Einstein’s equations is inextendible as a Lorentzian manifold in the above regularity class of course implies that it is also inextendible as a weak solution in the above regularity class. Assuming now that g∈C0g\in C^{0} and ∂g∈Lloc2\partial g\in L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}} is indeed the roughest regularity class for which a physical notion of weak solution exists22 2 It is conceivable that even weaker physical notions of weak solutions are emerging or establishing themselves. it follows that classical time-evolution terminates and that one has reached indeed the maximal extent of the classical solution. This is the first motivation for the study of inextendibility of Lorentzian manifolds with g∈C0g\in C^{0} and ∂g∈Lloc2\partial g\in L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}. The Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility results established in this paper are only one step in this direction. They should be seen as implying that the solution under consideration cannot be continued as a weak solution that is locally Lipschitz regular.

The second motivation, which is closely related to the first one, comes from the strong cosmic censorship conjecture, which roughly states that general relativity is generically a deterministic theory. A modern mathematical formulation is the following:

(1.4) The maximal globally hyperbolic development (MGHD) of generic compact or asymptotically flat initial data is inextendible as a weak solution to the Einstein equations.

The MGHD is the maximal development of the initial data which a priori can be guaranteed to be uniquely determined by the initial data. Any extension as a weak solution thereof is in general non-unique. It is in this way that conjecture (1.4) implies that general relativity is generically deterministic. It follows from the earlier discussion that under the assumption that g∈C0g\in C^{0} and ∂g∈Lloc2\partial g\in L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}} is the roughest regularity class for which a physical notion of weak solution exists, (1.4) is implied by

The maximal globally hyperbolic development of generic compact or asymptotically flat initial data is inextendible as a Lorentzian manifold with g∈C0g\in C^{0} and ∂g∈Lloc2\partial g\in L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}.

For further discussion of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture, references, and historical background we refer the reader to the introduction of [10].

The third motivation stems from the investigation of the physical and geometric structure and strength of spacetime singularities. According to relativistic point mechanics one can crudely identify the spacetime curvature with the tidal forces, the Levi-Civita connection with the gravito-inertial structure, and the spacetime metric with spatial and temporal distances. The statement that a singular spacetime is Cloc1,1C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible then corresponds to the statement that tidal forces blow up, a singularity which is Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible indicates the breakdown of the gravito-inertial structure, and a C0C^{0}-inextendibility result shows that the notion of space and time cannot be continued. Traditionally the investigation of the different structures of spacetime singularities was mainly at the level of curvature and its effect on Jacobi fields along incomplete timelike geodesics, cf. for example [38], [31]. Investigation at low-regularity level gives new information: in [37] it was shown that space itself is torn apart at the singularity inside a Schwarzschild black hole while a result of this paper is for example that there is no unique standard of finite inertial energy near a cosmological FLRW singularity with particle horizons. Indeed, in a sense made precise below the local gravitational energy diverges. The gravito-inertial structure of the Schwarzschild singularity is of similar nature.

1.2 Earlier works on low-regularity inextendibility

The first study of low-regularity inextendibility of Lorentzian manifolds was carried out in [37], where the C0C^{0}-inextendibility of the Minkowski spacetime and of the maximal analytic Schwarzschild spacetime was shown, see also [36]. A conditional C0C^{0}-inextendibility criterion for expanding singularities was given by Chruściel and Klinger in [5]. In [13] Galloway and Ling showed the C0C^{0}-inextendibility of the AdS spacetime and presented C0C^{0}-extendibility results for a class of hyperbolic FLRW spacetimes which they dubbed Milne-like. The latter results have been extended by Ling in [25]. In [14] it was shown that globally hyperbolic and timelike geodesically complete spacetimes are C0C^{0}-inextendible, a result which was improved in various directions first by Graf and Ling in [17] and finally by Minguzzi and Suhr in [28]. For an inextendibility result due to timelike geodesic completeness in Lorentzian length spaces by Grant, Kunzinger, and Sämann see [18].

1.3 Outline and discussion of main results

All of the previous studies of low-regularity inextendibility results captured geometric obstructions at the C0C^{0}-level. However, there are physical singularities which are Cloc1,1C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible due to blow-up of curvature but at the same time do admit continuous extensions. Perhaps most notably let us mention here the weak null singularities inside charged or rotating black holes33 3 For an overview of results and further references see the introduction of [26].. The singular behaviour happens there not already at the level of the metric but only at the level of the connection. This paper widens the geometric investigation of gravitational singularities to the level of the connection. We show how local holonomy transformations can be used to infer its blow-up.

Curvature and holonomy are of course intimately related. However, intuitively speaking, it depends on the ‘rate of the blow-up’ of curvature near a singularity whether the connection will also blow up or not44 4 A simple illustration is provided by the well-known exact impulsive gravitational wave spacetimes [32] where curvature has a delta singularity across a hypersurface but the Christoffel symbols are uniformly bounded.. One can think of holonomy as a geometric way to integrate curvature.

We proceed by giving a rough sketch of the proof of Theorem 1.1 in Section 3 which outlines the main idea of the argument. All the inextendibility proofs in this paper are by contradiction and have the following first step in common: assuming that there is a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} of (M,g)(M,g) one can find a timelike geodesic γ\gamma in MM which has a limit point q~\tilde{q} in M~∖ι⁡(M)\tilde{M}\setminus\iota(M), i.e., it leaves MM. Moreover one can find a small chart U~⊆M~\tilde{U}\subseteq\tilde{M} around q~\tilde{q} in which we have Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-control over the metric. In particular, in those coordinates the Christoffel symbols of gg in U~∩ι⁡(M)\tilde{U}\cap\iota(M) are uniformly bounded. Apart from the Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-control of the metric these results are valid also for C0C^{0}-extensions and are found in [37], [14], and [36]. They are here summarised in Section 2.2.

In Section 2.3 we prove a small lemma showing that if we have uniform bounds on the metric and its derivatives in some coordinate system as above, and if a curve is local in the sense that its coordinate velocity is uniformly bounded and also its domain of definition, then the parallel transport map along this curve is also uniformly bounded. This will be used to put upper bounds on holonomy transformations along curves in U~∩ι⁡(M)\tilde{U}\cap\iota(M) which are local in the above sense.

The third condition on the scale factor a⁡(t)a(t) in Theorem 1.1 guarantees that all future inextendible timelike geodesics in MM are future complete, and thus one can show that q~\tilde{q} cannot be a future endpoint ([14]). So it remains to show that q~\tilde{q} can neither be a past endpoint of γ\gamma. Here, the structure of the big-bang singularity enters. One first shows that the projection of geodesics in M=(0,∞)×M¯M=(0,\infty)\times\overline{M} to M¯\overline{M} are still geodesics, though not necessarily affinely parametrised. The second condition on the scale factor a⁡(t)a(t) in Theorem 1.1 expresses that particle horizons are present and thus the projection of γ\gamma to M¯\overline{M} has a limit point in M¯\overline{M}. Choosing polar normal coordinates (χ,θ,φ)(\chi,\theta,\varphi) around this limit point, in which the projected geodesic is a radial one, the timelike geodesic γ\gamma completely lies in the totally geodesic submanifold spanned by the tt and the radial χ\chi coordinate. Because the submanifold is totally geodesic parallel transport tangential to it in MM can be computed intrinsically in the submanifold. Thus we can reduce the problem in the following to a two-dimensional one with metric g|{t,χ}=−d​t2+a​(t)2​d​χ2g|_{\{t,\chi\}}=-dt^{2}+a(t)^{2}d\chi^{2}. Choosing now a base-point γ⁡(−μ)\gamma(-\mu) on γ\gamma we construct a family of loops as in Figure 3. Here, t^​(t)=∫0t1a⁡(t′)​d​t′\hat{t}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\frac{1}{a(t^{\prime})}\,dt^{\prime} is such that the metric in (t^,χ)(\hat{t},\chi)-coordinates becomes conformally flat, so that the diagram in Figure 3 is a Penrose diagram.

A loop in this family consists first of an outgoing null geodesic segment ℓ\ell, then concatenated with an ingoing one ℓ¯\underline{\ell} which brings us back to γ\gamma at a point γ⁡(−μ0)\gamma(-\mu_{0}), and then we go back along γ\gamma to γ⁡(−μ)\gamma(-\mu). The family of loops is indexed by the point γ⁡(−μ0)\gamma(-\mu_{0}) of return to γ\gamma. One can now show that the holonomy transformations at the base point γ⁡(−μ)\gamma(-\mu) associated with this family of loops form an unbounded family of boosts.

Using a homotopy argument and the causal nature of the loops one can show that all the loops in this family are local curves in U~∩ι⁡(M)\tilde{U}\cap\iota(M) in the sense discussed above. This gives the contradiction that the corresponding holonomy transformations should form a uniformly bounded subset of the Lorentz group.

We now briefly discuss the physical implication and interpretation of the unbounded holonomy transformations as above near the big-bang singularity. For this it is helpful to reverse the time-orientation for the time being and consider the inertial observer γ\gamma approaching the singularity. The inertial observer γ\gamma carries with himself his local orthonormal reference frame {f0=γ˙,f1,f2,f3}\{f_{0}=\dot{\gamma},f_{1},f_{2},f_{3}\}, where we can assume that f1f_{1} lies in the {t,χ}\{t,\chi\}-plane. By definition the local reference frame is parallel along γ\gamma. An equivalent statement to the unboundedness of the holonomy transformations with base point γ⁡(−μ)\gamma(-\mu) is thus that the parallel transport map along the null segments ℓ\ell and ℓ¯\underline{\ell} of the loop from γ⁡(−μ)\gamma(-\mu) to γ⁡(−μ0)\gamma(-\mu_{0}) is unbounded in the basis of the parallel frame (f0,f1,f2,f3)(f_{0},f_{1},f_{2},f_{3}) along γ\gamma as γ⁡(−μ0)\gamma(-\mu_{0}) approaches the singularity at {t^=0}\{\hat{t}=0\}. More precisely one can show that the parallel transport of the null vector −∂t^+∂χ-\partial_{\hat{t}}+\partial_{\chi} (which is tangent to ℓ¯\underline{\ell}) along the null segments ℓ\ell and ℓ¯\underline{\ell} becomes unbounded in the reference frame (f0,f1,f2,f3)(f_{0},f_{1},f_{2},f_{3}) along γ\gamma. This of course is a manifestation of the well-known red-shift effect in cosmology which turns into a blue-shift if we reverse the time-orientation. The parallel transport in regions bounded away from {t^=0}\{\hat{t}=0\} is of course uniformly bounded and thus the unbounded growth happens along the segment ℓ¯\underline{\ell} when it is approaching {t^=0}\{\hat{t}=0\}.

A physical scenario of unbounded local energy extraction from the gravitational field near such a singularity might now take the following form: using a finite amount of fuel the observer γ\gamma ejects a small probe σ\sigma which then sends radiation back to γ\gamma, see Figure 3. Using the geometric optics approximation (see for example [29] or [35]) it then follows that the energy of the radiation received by γ\gamma, which is proportional to minus the inner product of f0f_{0} and the parallely propagated null vector along ℓ¯\underline{\ell}, exceeds the energy he has put into the probe by an arbitrarily large amount.

In a second possible scenario the probe σ\sigma is first accelerated off γ\gamma and, after a while, it is accelerated back towards γ\gamma and then approaches γ\gamma on a timelike geodesic trajectory, see Figure 3. The closer the collision point of σ\sigma and γ\gamma is to the singularity, the larger the velocity of σ\sigma appears to γ\gamma, approaching the speed of light in the limit, see also Remark 3.14. Since the two phases of acceleration of σ\sigma are bounded away from t^=0\hat{t}=0, these accelerations require a uniformly bounded amount of fuel. On the other hand, the kinetic energy of σ\sigma gained from the perspective of γ\gamma can exceed this amount by an arbitrarily large quantity.

Let us remark that in this scenario we have of course reversed the time direction in order to be able to approach the big-bang singularity. However, we point out in Remark 3.16 that the Schwarzschild singularity exhibits a similar, although not identical, holonomy structure. It can be approached by a future-heading observer falling into the black hole and the above scenario can be transposed to this case.

This fits into a body of results which show/indicate that local forms of energy, and not just energy density, can diverge near a singularity, cf. for example [33], [21], [26], [12].

Motivated by the exhibited holonomy structure of the cosmological and the Schwarzschild singularities, we can define the geometric notion of the local causal holonomy associated with a timelike geodesic, which is a subset of the Lorentz group: Let (M,g)(M,g) be a time-oriented Lorentzian manifold and γ:[0,1)→M\gamma:[0,1)\to M a future directed and future inextendible timelike geodesic. Choose a point s0∈[0,1)s_{0}\in[0,1) and set

l.c.Hol(γ,s0):={Pσ∈O(1,3)(Tγ⁡(s0)M)| for some ​s1∈(s0,1)​ we have ​σ=γ|[s0,s1]←∗τ, with ​τ:[s0,s1]→M​ being causally homotopic  with fixed endpoints to γ|[s0,s1]}.\begin{split}l.c.Hol(\gamma,s_{0}):=\{P_{\sigma}\in O(1,3)(T_{\gamma(s_{0})}M)\;|\;&\textnormal{ for some }s_{1}\in(s_{0},1)\textnormal{ we have }\sigma=\overleftarrow{\gamma|_{[s_{0},s_{1}]}}*\tau\;,\\ &\textnormal{ with }\tau:[s_{0},s_{1}]\to M\textnormal{ being causally homotopic }\\ &\textnormal{ with fixed endpoints to }\gamma|_{[s_{0},s_{1}]}\}\;.\end{split}

Here, Pσ:Tγ⁡(s0)​M→Tγ⁡(s0)​MP_{\sigma}:T_{\gamma(s_{0})}M\to T_{\gamma(s_{0})}M denotes the parallel transport map along the loop σ\sigma, O​(1,3)​(Tγ⁡(s0)​M)O(1,3)(T_{\gamma(s_{0})}M) denotes the group of Lorentz transformations on Tγ⁡(s0)​MT_{\gamma(s_{0})}M, γ|[s0,s1]←\overleftarrow{\gamma|_{[s_{0},s_{1}]}} denotes the reversal of γ|[s0,s1]\gamma|_{[s_{0},s_{1}]}, and a causal homotopy with fixed endpoints is a homotopy with fixed endpoints via causal curves, see also Lemma 2.12. If γ\gamma is chosen to approach the Schwarzschild singularity, or, after reversal of time-orientation, γ\gamma is chosen to approach a cosmological big-bang singularity as above, then in both cases and for all s0∈[0,1)s_{0}\in[0,1) we have that l.c.H​o​l​(γ,s0)l.c.Hol(\gamma,s_{0}) is a subset of O​(1,3)​(Tγ⁡(s0)​M)O(1,3)(T_{\gamma(s_{0})}M) with non-compact closure.

We now discuss the weak null singularities and the proof of Theorem 1.2 in Section 4.1 by contrasting it with the much cleaner/simpler case of the cosmological singularities. The strategy of the proof is similar, one again assumes that there exists a future Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension and then finds a future directed timelike geodesic γ\gamma which leaves the original spacetime (M,g)(M,g) for the extension (M~,g~)(\tilde{M},\tilde{g}) through a boundary point around which one has Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-control over the metric g~\tilde{g} in a small coordinate neighbourhood. In the cosmological case one could now directly go over to a two-dimensional problem which is not possible here. Another difference to the cosmological case is that the analogous construction of the loops from broken null geodesics gives a uniformly bounded holonomy. In fact, broken timelike geodesics do not work either. This is a manifestation of the fact that unlike in the cosmological case (cf. Remark 3.14) there is only one standard of finite inertial energy at the weak null singularity. We proceed as follows: using homotopy arguments we show that one can also find a radially outgoing null geodesic τ\tau in MM which leaves for the extension. Assume without loss of generality that τ\tau approaches the singularity {v=0}\{v=0\}, i.e., τ\tau is tangent to ∂v\partial_{v}. We then construct a family of mixed-null-and-spacelike loops based at a point of τ\tau near the singularity {v=0}\{v=0\} by first moving briefly in the angular φ\varphi direction on the spheres 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2}, then moving only in vv towards the singularity, moving back in φ\varphi and returning by moving back in vv, cf. also Figure 9 on page 9. One can show that the holonomy along those loops becomes unbounded when they approach the singularity at {v=0}\{v=0\}. It remains to show that these loops are local in the sense discussed earlier, which is not as straightforward as in the cosmological case. For this we also make use of the affine structure.

One could also define a geometric quantity in the case of the weak null singularities which becomes unbounded, although it is more complicated than the local causal holonomy defined earlier. The interested reader however can easily construct such a quantity from the proof in Section 4.1.

As a first self-contained example of a (non-bifurcate) weak null singularity to which our Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility result applies we give the Reissner-Nordström-Vaidya (RNV) spacetime in Section 4.2, which models the influx of null-dust into a subextremal Reissner-Nordström black hole. This model has been the earliest exact-solution model used to understand the singularity forming at the Cauchy horizon of dynamical charged or rotating black holes, see [23]. In [21] an argument has been made for an infinite energy transfer from the gravitational field near such a singularity to test bodies. We also point out here that the Hawking mass remains uniformly bounded at the Cauchy horizon of the RNV spacetime and that our Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility result does not require mass-inflation ([33], [34], [30]) as an assumption.

Our main application of Theorem 1.2 is in Section 4.3 to spacetimes arising from generic and sufficiently small spherically symmetric perturbations of asymptotically flat two-ended subextremal Reissner-Nordström initial data for the Einstein-Maxwell-scalar field system as studied by Luk and Oh in [26], [27]. Their work builds up on results by Dafermos [7], [8], [9] and Dafermos-Rodnianski [11]. A Penrose diagram of those spacetimes is given in Figure 12 on page 12 and we refer the reader to [26] for a detailed discussion. In [26], [27] Luk and Oh prove the C2C^{2}-formulation of strong cosmic censorship for this class of spacetimes. Based on their work we improve this to a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-formulation in this paper: it can be directly inferred from the estimates in [26] that the interior of the black hole satisfies the assumptions in Theorem 1.2 and is thus future Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible. In the appendix of this paper we show that the exterior of the black hole is timelike geodesically complete in the sense that any future inextendible timelike geodesic starting in the exterior is either future complete or enters the black hole interior. This then suffices to infer the global Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility of the spacetime and thus the Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-formulation of strong cosmic censorship.

Other (closely related) examples of spherically symmetric weak null singularities to which our results apply are those constructed in [39] for the Einstein-Maxwell-charged scalar field sysytem and in [6] for the Einstein-Maxwell-scalar field system with a positive cosmological constant.

Let us conclude the introduction by remarking that we do not attempt in this paper to define precisely what we mean by a holonomy singularity in general, since we expect that they can come in various forms still to be explored. As we have seen, the holonomy structures of the cosmological singularities considered and the weak null singularities are already very different.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Preliminary definitions

Let MM be a smooth (d+1)(d+1)-dimensional manifold55 5 We will always assume in this paper that manifolds are smooth. Recall that a C1C^{1}-structure on a manifold can always be refined to a smooth structure, see also the related Remark 2.2.. We briefly recall that a Lorentzian metric gg on MM is locally Lipschitz regular (or Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-regular) iff for all smooth charts ψ:M⊇U→V⊆ℝd+1\psi:M\supseteq U\to V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d+1} the coordinate expressions of the metric gμ​ν∘ψ−1:ℝd+1⊇V→ℝg_{\mu\nu}\circ\psi^{-1}:\mathbb{R}^{d+1}\supseteq V\to\mathbb{R} are locally Lipschitz, i.e., for all compact sets K⊆VK\subseteq V there exists a constant Λ⁡(K)>0\Lambda(K)>0 such that for all x,y∈Kx,y\in K we have

|(gμ​ν∘ψ−1)​(x)−(gμ​ν∘ψ−1)​(y)|≤Λ⁡(K)​‖x−y‖ℝd+1.|(g_{\mu\nu}\circ\psi^{-1})(x)-(g_{\mu\nu}\circ\psi^{-1})(y)|\leq\Lambda(K)||x-y||_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}}\;.

Here, ‖x−y‖ℝd+1||x-y||_{\mathbb{R}^{d+1}} denotes the coordinate distance of xx and yy in ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1}, which, if VV is not convex, is not necessarily the distance of xx and yy in V⊆ℝd+1V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d+1}. However, it is not difficult to show that a function f:ℝd+1⊇V→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d+1}\supseteq V\to\mathbb{R} is locally Lipschitz with respect to the ambient distance function of ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1} if, and only if, it is locally Lipschitz with respect to the intrinsic distance function of VV (although the optimal Lipschitz constant will be different in general). Thus, both possible definitions give rise to the same class of functions.

Similarly, one defines a locally Lipschitz curve in MM or, in general, locally Lipschitz maps between manifolds. Note that all these definitions are independent of a distance function on MM but only depend on the smooth structure.

Definition 2.1.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a smooth Lorentzian manifold and let Γ\Gamma be a regularity class, for example Γ=Ck\Gamma=C^{k} with k∈ℕ∪{∞}k\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\} or Γ=Cloc0,1\Gamma=C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}. A Γ\Gamma-extension of (M,g)(M,g) consists of a smooth isometric embedding ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} of MM into a Lorentzian manifold (M~,g~)(\tilde{M},\tilde{g}) of the same dimension as MM where g~\tilde{g} is Γ\Gamma-regular and such that ∂ι⁡(M)⊆M~\partial\iota(M)\subseteq\tilde{M} is non-empty.

If (M,g)(M,g) admits a Γ\Gamma-extension, then we say that (M,g)(M,g) is Γ\Gamma-extendible, otherwise we say (M,g)(M,g) is Γ\Gamma-inextendbile.

Remark 2.2.

Recall that the question of extendibility of Lorentzian manifolds is motivated by the physical question of whether spacetime can be continued. In the process of the mathematical modelling one might wonder whether one gains continuability by also lowering the regularity of the differentiable structure of the manifold itself in the above definition. But indeed this is not the case as long as one does not go below a C1C^{1}-differentiable structure, which is needed for the existence of a continuous tangent space and the notion of a continuous Lorentzian metric. To see this, let MM be a smooth manifold, gg a smooth Lorentzian metric on MM, M~\tilde{M} a C1C^{1} manifold with a C0C^{0} Lorentzian metric g~\tilde{g} and let ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} be a C1C^{1} isometric embedding. Then ι\iota induces on ι⁡(M)⊆M~\iota(M)\subseteq\tilde{M} a smooth structure which is compatible with the given C1C^{1} structure on ι⁡(M)\iota(M) and with respect to which g~|ι⁡(M)\tilde{g}|_{\iota(M)} is smooth. The proof of Theorem 2.9 in Chapter 2 of [22] shows that this smooth structure can be extended to a smooth one on all of M~\tilde{M} which is compatible with the given C1C^{1} structure – thus turning M~\tilde{M} into a smooth manifold and ι\iota into a smooth isometric embedding, and thus recovering the stronger assumptions in the above definition.

Let now (M,g)(M,g) be a Lorentzian manifold with a continuous metric. In this paper we use the convention that a timelike curve is a piecewise smooth curve which has a timelike tangent everywhere – and at the points of discontinuity of the tangent the right and left tangent vectors lie in the same connectedness component of the timelike double cone of tangent vectors. Similarly we define a causal curve as a piecewise C1C^{1} curve which has a causal, non-vanishing tangent everywhere – and at points of discontinuity of the tangent the right and left tangent vectors lie in the same connectedness component of the causal double cone of tangent vectors with the origin removed. Let (M,g)(M,g) be in addition time-oriented. For p∈Mp\in M we denote the timelike future of pp in MM by I+​(p,M)I^{+}(p,M), which is the set of all points q∈Mq\in M such that there is a future directed timelike curve from pp to qq. The causal future of pp in MM, denoted by J+​(p,M)J^{+}(p,M), is the set which contains pp and all points q∈Mq\in M such that there is a future directed causal curve from pp to qq. The sets I−​(p,M)I^{-}(p,M) and J−​(p,M)J^{-}(p,M) are defined analogously.

Note that for Lorentzian manifolds with a merely continuous metric there are good reasons for defining timelike and causal curves as locally Lipschitz curves with a timelike or causal tangent almost everywhere, which also leads to different causal sets, cf. [4], [19]. However this is not needed for our purposes.

2.2 Fundamentals of C0C^{0}-extensions

We now recall some fundamental definitions and results for C0C^{0}-extensions.

Definition 2.3.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian manifold and ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} a C0C^{0}-extension of MM. The future boundary of MM is the set ∂+ι⁡(M)\partial^{+}\iota(M) consisting of all points p~∈M~\tilde{p}\in\tilde{M} such that there exists a smooth timelike curve γ~:[−1,0]→M~\tilde{\gamma}:[-1,0]\to\tilde{M} such that Im(γ~|[−1,0))⊆ι(M)\mathrm{Im}(\tilde{\gamma}|_{[-1,0)})\subseteq\iota(M), γ~​(0)=p~∈∂ι⁡(M)\tilde{\gamma}(0)=\tilde{p}\in\partial\iota(M), and ι−1∘γ~|[−1,0)\iota^{-1}\circ\tilde{\gamma}|_{[-1,0)} is future directed in MM.

Clearly we have ∂+ι⁡(M)⊆∂ι⁡(M)\partial^{+}\iota(M)\subseteq\partial\iota(M). The past boundary ∂−ι⁡(M)\partial^{-}\iota(M) is defined analogously.

Definition 2.4.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian manifold and let Γ\Gamma be a regularity class that is equal to or stronger than C0C^{0}. A future Γ\Gamma-extension of (M,g)(M,g) is a Γ\Gamma-extension ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} of MM with ∂+ι⁡(M)≠∅\partial^{+}\iota(M)\neq\emptyset. If no such extension exists, then (M,g)(M,g) is said to be future Γ\Gamma-inextendible.

Past Γ\Gamma-extensions are defined analogously. The next lemma is a reformulation of Lemma 2.17 in [37].

Lemma 2.5.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian manifold and ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} a C0C^{0}-extension of MM. Then ∂+ι⁡(M)∪∂−ι⁡(M)≠∅\partial^{+}\iota(M)\cup\partial^{-}\iota(M)\neq\emptyset.

In particular the Lemma shows that if (M,g)(M,g) is future and past Γ\Gamma-inextendible, then it is also Γ\Gamma-inextendible.

The past and future boundary interchange under a change of time orientation of (M,g)(M,g). It is thus sufficient to focus in the following on the future boundary. The next proposition is found in [36], Proposition 2.2.

We briefly elaborate on the statement of this lemma. We recall that the causal relations are global in nature. Given a causal curve σ\sigma in MM from γ⁡(0)\gamma(0) to γ⁡(1)\gamma(1), then ι∘σ\iota\circ\sigma lies by definition in J+​(γ~​(0),M~)∩J−​(γ~​(1),M~)J^{+}(\tilde{\gamma}(0),\tilde{M})\cap J^{-}(\tilde{\gamma}(1),\tilde{M}), but in general it does not have to lie in J+​(γ~​(0),U~)∩J−​(γ~​(1),U~)J^{+}(\tilde{\gamma}(0),\tilde{U})\cap J^{-}(\tilde{\gamma}(1),\tilde{U}), even if the latter set is compact in U~\tilde{U}. In applications U~\tilde{U} will be chosen to be a small neighbourhood of γ\gamma and thus the lemma shows that causal curves that are causally homotopic to γ\gamma belong to the local causality of U~\tilde{U}. Related techniques have already been employed by the author in [37].

Since s↦(ι∘Γ)​(s,rn)s\mapsto(\iota\circ\Gamma)(s;r_{n}) is a future directed causal curve in U~\tilde{U} from γ~​(0)\tilde{\gamma}(0) to γ~​(1)\tilde{\gamma}(1), it lies in J+​(γ~​(0),U~)∩J−​(γ~​(1),U~)J^{+}(\tilde{\gamma}(0),\tilde{U})\cap J^{-}(\tilde{\gamma}(1),\tilde{U}). Since this set is compactly contained in U~\tilde{U} by assumption, it follows that also s↦(ι∘Γ)​(s,r∞)s\mapsto(\iota\circ\Gamma)(s;r_{\infty}) maps into U~\tilde{U}. This shows that I=[0,1]I=[0,1], which concludes the proof. ∎

2.3 Lemma for bounding local holonomy in Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extensions

The following lemma is fundamental to all our later applications.

We remark that the Schwarzschild singularity is also a holonomy singularity: Consider the interior (M,g)(M,g) of the Schwarzschild solution, where M=ℝ×(0,2​m)×𝕊2M=\mathbb{R}\times(0,2m)\times\mathbb{S}^{2} with standard (t,r,θ,φ)(t,r,\theta,\varphi)-coordinates and g=−(1−2​mr)​d​t2+11−2​mr​d​r2+r2​(d​θ2+sin2⁡θ​d​φ2)g=-(1-\frac{2m}{r})\,dt^{2}+\frac{1}{1-\frac{2m}{r}}\,dr^{2}+r^{2}(d\theta^{2}+\sin^{2}\theta\,d\varphi^{2}). We define an orthonormal basis by e0:=−(2​mr−1)1/2∂re_{0}:=-(\frac{2m}{r}-1)^{\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}}\,\partial_{r}, e1:=(2​mr−1)−1/2∂te_{1}:=(\frac{2m}{r}-1)^{-\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}}\,\partial_{t}, e2:=1r∂θe_{2}:=\frac{1}{r}\,\partial_{\theta}, e3:=1r​sin⁡θ∂φe_{3}:=\frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\,\partial_{\varphi}. Note that this frame is parallel along e0e_{0} and that the {t,r}\{t,r\}-plane as well as the {r,θ}\{r,\theta\}-plane are totally geodesic. We also have future particle horizons. For simplicity we restrict our consideration here to an observer with affine velocity vector e0e_{0}.

Let us consider first a null basis L=e0+e1L=e_{0}+e_{1} and L¯=e0−e1\underline{L}=e_{0}-e_{1} for the {t,r}\{t,r\}-plane. A straightforward computation now yields ∇L(r2​m−r​L)=0\nabla_{L}(\frac{\sqrt{r}}{\sqrt{2m-r}}L)=0 and ∇L(2​m−rr​L¯)=0\nabla_{L}(\frac{\sqrt{2m-r}}{\sqrt{r}}\underline{L})=0, which shows that light propagating in the LL-direction is infinitely red-shifted when approaching r=0r=0 as observed by our observer, as expected from the infinite expansion in the tt-direction. Note that this is different to the situation of the cosmological singularities we just discussed, where we encounter an infinite blue-shift of radiation approaching the singularity. However, now the parallel transport of L¯\underline{L} along LL blows up when approaching r=0r=0.

Considering the situation in the {r,θ}\{r,\theta\}-plane, we set ℓ:=e0+e2\ell:=e_{0}+e_{2} and ℓ¯:=e0−e2\underline{\ell}:=e_{0}-e_{2}. A computation gives ∇ℓ(1r​ℓ)=0\nabla_{\ell}(\frac{1}{r}\ell)=0, which shows that we have an infinite blue-shift of radiation travelling in ℓ\ell-direction when approaching r=0r=0 as observed by our observer, in qualitatively the same manner as in the cosmological singularities discussed earlier.

With a bit of additional work one can now extend the method of proof of Theorem 3.7 also to the Schwarzschild singularity, showing Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility. But of course this statement is strictly weaker than the C0C^{0}-inextendibility proven in [37]. However, the blow-up of the local causal holonomy is of independent interest.

Theorem 3.5 and Theorem 3.7 together directly give the following

Corollary 3.17.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a cosmological warped product spacetime with b=∞b=\infty and let the scale factor a:(0,∞)→(0,∞)a:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty) satisfy limt→0a⁡(t)=0\lim_{t\to 0}a(t)=0, ∫1∞a⁡(t)a​(t)2+1​𝑑t=∞\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{a(t)}{\sqrt{a(t)^{2}+1}}\,dt=\infty and ∫011a⁡(t′)​d​t′<∞\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{a(t^{\prime})}\,dt^{\prime}<\infty. Then (M,g)(M,g) is Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible.

The physically most interesting examples of cosmological warped product spacetimes, and thus the physically most relevant application of Theorem 3.5, Theorem 3.7, and Corollary 3.17, are to the class of isotropic and homogeneous cosmological models, known as FLRW spacetimes. Here, (M¯K,g¯K)(\overline{M}_{K},\overline{g}_{K}) is a 33-dimensional complete Riemannian manifold of constant sectional curvature KK. By redefining the scale factor function a⁡(t)a(t) one may restrict to the three cases K=−1,0,+1K=-1,0,+1. In all three cases one can locally introduce polar normal coordinates1515 15 See for example [24], Chapter 10. (χ,θ,φ)∈(0,χ0)×𝕊2(\chi,\theta,\varphi)\in(0,\chi_{0})\times\mathbb{S}^{2} on M¯K\overline{M}_{K} such that the 33-metric in these coordinates reads

g¯K=d​χ2+fK​(χ)2​(d​θ2+sin2⁡θ​d​φ2) with {fK​(χ)=sinh⁡χ for ​K=−1fK​(χ)=χ for ​K=0fK​(χ)=sin⁡χ for ​K=+1.\overline{g}_{K}=d\chi^{2}+f_{K}(\chi)^{2}(d\theta^{2}+\sin^{2}\theta\,d\varphi^{2})\quad\textnormal{ with }\quad\begin{cases}f_{K}(\chi)=\sinh\chi\qquad&\textnormal{ for }K=-1\\ f_{K}(\chi)=\chi&\textnormal{ for }K=0\\ f_{K}(\chi)=\sin\chi&\textnormal{ for }K=+1\;.\end{cases}

Thus, in the coordinates (t,χ,θ,φ)(t,\chi,\theta,\varphi) the spacetime metric reads

g=−d​t2+a​(t)2​[d​χ2+fK​(χ)2​(d​θ2+sin2⁡θ​d​φ2)].g=-dt^{2}+a(t)^{2}\big[d\chi^{2}+f_{K}(\chi)^{2}(d\theta^{2}+\sin^{2}\theta\,d\varphi^{2})\big]\;.

Note that various topologies are possible for M¯K\overline{M}_{K}. The classical, simply connected choices are M¯−1=M¯0=ℝ3\overline{M}_{-1}=\overline{M}_{0}=\mathbb{R}^{3} with almost global coordinates (χ,θ,φ)∈(0,∞)×(0,π)×(0,2​π)(\chi,\theta,\varphi)\in(0,\infty)\times(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi), and M¯1=𝕊3\overline{M}_{1}=\mathbb{S}^{3} with almost global coordinates (χ,θ,φ)∈(0,π)×(0,π)×(0,2​π)(\chi,\theta,\varphi)\in(0,\pi)\times(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi).

Theorem 4.1.

Then there exists no Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} with the property that there is a future directed future inextendible timelike geodesic γ:[−1,0)→M\gamma:[-1,0)\to M with lims→0v⁡(γ⁡(s))=0\lim_{s\to 0}v(\gamma(s))=0 and such that lims→0(ι∘γ)​(s)\lim_{s\to 0}(\iota\circ\gamma)(s) exists in M~\tilde{M}.

  1. 1.

    Note that the theorem does not require the Hawking mass to go to infinity for v→0v\to 0.

  3. 3.

    The Theorem remains valid for a much larger class of spacetimes. For the proof, as written, to go through it suffices that in addition to the first two bullet points one assumes that for each u0∈(−∞,0)u_{0}\in(-\infty,0) there exists a sequence vn∈(−∞,0)v_{n}\in(-\infty,0) with vn→0v_{n}\to 0 for n→∞n\to\infty such that (∂ur⋅∂vr)​(u0,vn)>0(\partial_{u}r\cdot\partial_{v}r)(u_{0},v_{n})>0 and, moreover, such that |∂ur⁡(u0,vn)|→∞|\partial_{u}r(u_{0},v_{n})|\to\infty or |∂vr⁡(u0,vn)|→∞|\partial_{v}r(u_{0},v_{n})|\to\infty for n→∞n\to\infty. We would expect that one can in addition remove the assumption on the sign of ∂ur⋅∂vr\partial_{u}r\cdot\partial_{v}r, but this would require a modification of the proof. All of the physically interesting applications known to the author are however covered by the assumptions made in the theorem.

4.2 Reissner-Nordström-Vaidya spacetimes

The Reissner-Nordström-Vaidya (RNV) spacetime (M,g)(M,g) is given by M=ℝ×(0,∞)×𝕊2M=\mathbb{R}\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb{S}^{2} with canonical (v,r)(v,r)-coordinates on the first two factors and

(4.18) g=−(1−2​ϖ​(v)r+e2r2)​d​v2+d​v⊗d​r+d​r⊗d​v+r2​γ̊,g=-\Big(1-\frac{2\varpi(v)}{r}+\frac{e^{2}}{r^{2}}\Big)\,dv^{2}+dv\otimes dr+dr\otimes dv+r^{2}\,\mathring{\gamma}\;,

where e>0e>0 and ϖ:ℝ→(0,∞)\varpi:\mathbb{R}\to(0,\infty) is a smooth non-decreasing function, [1]. Together with the Maxwell field F:=2​er2​d​v∧d​rF:=\frac{2e}{r^{2}}\,dv\wedge dr and ρ:=1r2​∂vϖ≥0\rho:=\frac{1}{r^{2}}\partial_{v}\varpi\geq 0, and defining the stress-energy tensor Tμ​νem=Fμ​λ​Fνλ−12​gμ​ν​Fλ​ρ​Fλ​ρT^{\mathrm{em}}_{\mu\nu}=F_{\mu\lambda}F_{\nu}^{\;\;\lambda}-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}F_{\lambda\rho}F^{\lambda\rho} of the electromagnetic field and the stress-energy tensor Tμ​νdust=ρ⋅∂μv​∂νvT^{\mathrm{dust}}_{\mu\nu}=\rho\cdot\partial_{\mu}v\partial_{\nu}v of dust, it solves the Einstein-Maxwell-null-dust equations

Rμ​ν−12​gμ​ν​R\displaystyle R_{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}R =2​(Tμ​νem+Tμ​νdust)\displaystyle=2(T^{\mathrm{em}}_{\mu\nu}+T^{\mathrm{dust}}_{\mu\nu})
d​F\displaystyle dF =0,∇μFμ​ν=0\displaystyle=0\;,\qquad\nabla^{\mu}F_{\mu\nu}=0
∇μTμ​νdust\displaystyle\nabla^{\mu}T^{\mathrm{dust}}_{\mu\nu} =0,g−1(dv,dv)=0.\displaystyle=0\;,\qquad g^{-1}(dv,dv)=0\;.

A time orientation is fixed by stipulating that −∂r-\partial_{r} is future directed. We assume ϖ⁡(v)=ϖ⁡(∞)−β​v−p\varpi(v)=\varpi(\infty)-\beta v^{-p}, where β>0\beta>0, p>1p>1, and ϖ⁡(∞)>e>0\varpi(\infty)>e>0, and restrict our considerations to v≥v0v\geq v_{0}, where v0>0v_{0}>0 is so large that ϖ⁡(v0)>e\varpi(v_{0})>e. Thus, for late affine time vv the RNV spacetime we are considering models the continuous influx of null-dust into a sub-extremal Reissner-Nordström black hole decaying with a tail ρ∼v−(p+1)\rho\sim v^{-(p+1)}. A Penrose diagram is given in Figure 10.

In the following we introduce spherically symmetric double null coordinates (u,v)(u,v) on the RNV spacetime, see also Appendix B of [34]. Such coordinates are in particular used to infer the structure of the above Penrose diagram. Note however that in general no closed form solution exists for the second null coordinate uu. We construct it by the method of characteristics, prescribing initial values on {v=v0}\{v=v_{0}\}. We then focus on the region uℋ+<u<uTu_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}<u<u_{T}, which is defined by the property that outgoing null rays are eventually trapped. One can in fact show that every outgoing null ray starting inside the black hole is eventually trapped, see Proposition 4.29, and thus uTu_{T} corresponds to the left endpoint of the domain of definition of the null coordinate uu, cf. Figure 10. In Proposition 4.25 we show that for any u~∈(uℋ+,uT)\tilde{u}\in(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}},u_{T}) the region (uℋ+,u~)×(v0,∞)(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}},\tilde{u})\times(v_{0},\infty) satisfies the assumptions of Theorem 4.1, and thus the part of 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+} which is covered by the null coordinate uu is Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible in the precise sense of Theorem 4.1. One can now construct another null coordinate uu in the same way with initial values prescribed on {v=v1>v0}\{v=v_{1}>v_{0}\} to cover a larger part of 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+}. In this way it follows that all of 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+} is Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible in the sense of Theorem 4.1.

We now begin. Let f=1−2​ϖ​(v)r+e2r2f=1-\frac{2\varpi(v)}{r}+\frac{e^{2}}{r^{2}}. Then ℓ:=−∂∂r\ell:=-\frac{\partial}{\partial r} is future directed ingoing null and ℓ¯:=∂∂v+f2​∂∂r\underline{\ell}:=\frac{\partial}{\partial v}+\frac{f}{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r} is future directed outgoing null. We construct a null coordinate uu using the method of characteristics: on {v=v0}\{v=v_{0}\} we set u|{v=v0}=−ru|_{\{v=v_{0}\}}=-r and extend it by requiring that it is constant along the integral curves of ℓ¯\underline{\ell}.2323 23 Note that a priori this does not yield a globally defined function – and indeed the top left corner of the Penrose diagram will not be covered. The integral curves of ℓ¯\underline{\ell} are determined by

Defining the regions

we thus have f⁡(v,r)>0f(v,r)>0 on I∪I​I​II\cup III and f⁡(v,r)<0f(v,r)<0 and I​III. Furthermore, we have f⁡(v,r)=0f(v,r)=0 on the transition curves v↦(v,r−​(v))v\mapsto(v,r_{-}(v)) and v↦(v,r+​(v))v\mapsto(v,r_{+}(v)), which are the apparent horizons.

Claim 1: The integral curves of ℓ¯\underline{\ell} exist for all v≥v0v\geq v_{0}.

Proof.

For the ODE (4.19) to break down in finite affine time v≥v0v\geq v_{0} we must either have that rr goes to zero or infinity in finite affine time. Since we have ∂r∂v|u=f2>0\frac{\partial r}{\partial v}\Big|_{u}=\frac{f}{2}>0 in I​I​IIII, we cannot have r→0r\to 0. Moreover, it follows that rr is uniformly bounded from below along each integral curve, which directly implies that ff is uniformly bounded from above, and thus rr cannot go to infinity in finite affine time. ∎

Recall that r⁡(u,v)r(u,v) is the value of rr at affine time vv along the integral curve of ℓ¯\underline{\ell} that passes through (v=v0,r=−u)(v=v_{0},r=-u).

f⁡(v,r)=1r2​(r−r+​(v))​(r−r−​(v))≥1r2​(r−r+​(∞))​(r−r+​(∞))=(1−r+​(∞)r)2≥(1−r+​(∞)r1)2>0.f(v,r)=\frac{1}{r^{2}}(r-r_{+}(v))(r-r_{-}(v))\geq\frac{1}{r^{2}}(r-r_{+}(\infty))(r-r_{+}(\infty))=(1-\frac{r_{+}(\infty)}{r})^{2}\geq(1-\frac{r_{+}(\infty)}{r_{1}})^{2}>0\;.

Let us now define

We also define the asymptotic surface gravity of the event horizon by

(4.23) κ+​(∞):=r+​(∞)−r−​(∞)2​r+2​(∞)=12​∂rf⁡(∞,r+​(∞))=1r+2​(∞)​(ϖ⁡(∞)−e2r+​(∞)),\kappa_{+}(\infty):=\frac{r_{+}(\infty)-r_{-}(\infty)}{2r_{+}^{2}(\infty)}=\frac{1}{2}\partial_{r}f(\infty,r_{+}(\infty))=\frac{1}{r_{+}^{2}(\infty)}\big(\varpi(\infty)-\frac{e^{2}}{r_{+}(\infty)}\big)\;,

where the last two equalities follow easily from (4.2).

Then there exists u1>uℋ+u_{1}>u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}} with lim supv→∞r⁡(u1,v)≥r+​(∞)\limsup_{v\to\infty}r(u_{1},v)\geq r_{+}(\infty). for all u∈[uℋ+,u1]u\in[u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}},u_{1}] and v≥v1v\geq v_{1}, which, after integration in uu, is a contradiction to limv→∞r⁡(u,v)=r+​(∞)\lim_{v\to\infty}r(u,v)=r_{+}(\infty) for all u∈[uℋ+,u1]u\in[u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}},u_{1}]. ∎

Let Δ1>0\Delta_{1}>0 be such that r⁡(uℋ++Δ1,v0)∈(r−​(v0),r+​(v0))r(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}+\Delta_{1},v_{0})\in(r_{-}(v_{0}),r_{+}(v_{0})). We in particular show now that there is a small trapped neighbourhood towards the future of the event horizon, cf. Figure 10.

If we have r⁡(u,v0)∈(r−​(v0),r+​(v0))r(u,v_{0})\in(r_{-}(v_{0}),r_{+}(v_{0})) then this follows from Claim 3 and if r⁡(u,v0)∈(0,r−​(v0)]r(u,v_{0})\in(0,r_{-}(v_{0})] then there are two possibilities: Either r⁡(u,v)r(u,v) enters the region (r−​(v),r+​(v))(r_{-}(v),r_{+}(v)) at some later time, and then we use Claim 3 again, or we have r⁡(u,v)∈(0,r−​(v)]r(u,v)\in(0,r_{-}(v)] for all vv. If we had limv→∞r⁡(u,v)<r+​(∞)\lim_{v\to\infty}r(u,v)<r_{+}(\infty), then the right hand side of (4.20) would be positively bounded away from zero which would lead to the contradiction limv→∞r⁡(u,v)=∞\lim_{v\to\infty}r(u,v)=\infty. Thus we have limv→∞r⁡(u,v)=r−​(∞)\lim_{v\to\infty}r(u,v)=r_{-}(\infty).

We now show that for each u0∈(uℋ+,0)u_{0}\in(u_{\mathcal{H}^{+}},0) there exists a v1≥v0v_{1}\geq v_{0} such that ∂vr⁡(u0,v1)<0\partial_{v}r(u_{0},v_{1})<0 (and thus also ∂vr⁡(u0,v)<0\partial_{v}r(u_{0},v)<0 for all v≥v1v\geq v_{1} by Claim 3). Assume this were not the case, then ∂vr⁡(u0,v)≥0\partial_{v}r(u_{0},v)\geq 0 for all v≥v0v\geq v_{0}. Using the evolution equation for ∂vr\partial_{v}r from the first line of (4.28) we can then estimate

which is negative for large vv and thus a contradiction to ∂vr⁡(u0,v)≥0\partial_{v}r(u_{0},v)\geq 0 for all v≥v0v\geq v_{0}. ∎

4.3 Dafermos-Luk-Oh spacetimes and a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-result of strong cosmic censorship

Our next application of the Theorems 4.1 and 4.3 is to spacetimes arising from sufficiently small spherically symmetric perturbations of asymptotically flat two-ended subextremal Reissner-Nordström (RN) initial data for the Einstein-Maxwell-scalar field system, which we call Dafermos-Luk-Oh (DLO) spacetimes. The mathematical study of spherically symmetric perturbations of the interior of a subextremal RN black hole was initiated by Dafermos in [7], [8] where he in particular showed that if the perturbation decays sufficiently quickly along the event horizon that the metric then extends continuously to the Cauchy horizon in a small neighbourhood of timelike infinity. This sufficiently quick decay for spherically symmetric perturbations of RN initial data was later established by Dafermos and Rodnianski in [11]. Moreover, [8] also showed that if the scalar field is in addition pointwise polynomially lower bounded along the event horizon, then the Hawking mass and −∂vr-\partial_{v}r blow up on the Cauchy horizon near timelike infinity. Using a Cauchy stability argument and using the previous results Dafermos continued to show in [9] that for sufficiently small perturbations of two-ended subextremal RN initial data the Penrose diagram of the future development is as in Figure 12, i.e., the Cauchy horizon is given by a bifurcate null hypersurface as in exact subextremal RN. Moreover, the metric extends continuously to the Cauchy horizon.

In [27] Luk and Oh established that for generic small spherically symmetric perturbations the scalar field obeys an integrated lower bound along the event horizon. ‘Generic’ means here that the initial data is contained in an open and dense set relative to appropriate topologies of the initial data space. The integrated lower bound being weaker than the pointwise lower bound assumed in [8], Luk and Oh continued to show in [26] that it is still strong enough to ensure the blow-up of the energy of the scalar field near the Cauchy horizon which they then use to infer the generic C2C^{2}-inextendibility of the DLO spacetimes.2929 29 It should be mentioned that in [26] Luk and Oh do not only consider globally small perturbations of subextremal RN initial data that lead to what we call here an DLO spacetime, but they also treat ‘admissible’ large deviations from exact RN which possibly lead to the closing off of the Cauchy horizon, transitioning into a spacelike singularity in the interior. We do not discuss the latter case in detail here, but Theorem 4.1 can still be used to infer the Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility of the Cauchy horizon in the sense of Theorem 4.1. However, we do not investigate the low-regularity inextendibility of the spacelike part of the boundary in this paper. In particular Luk and Oh also show the pointwise blow up of −∂vr-\partial_{v}r on the Cauchy horizon, which allows us to infer the following

Theorem 4.30.

Consider a sufficiently small spherically symmetric perturbation of asymptotically flat two-ended subextremal RN initial data for the Einstein-Maxwell-scalar field system such that the future development is given by Figure 12. Assume the initial data is generic and small in the sense of [27]. Then the interior of the black hole3030 30 I.e. the set in Figure 12 bounded by the two C​H+CH^{+} to the future and the two ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} and part of the initial Cauchy hypersurface to the past. is future Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible.

Proof.

This follows directly from Theorem 4.3: By Theorem 5.5 and Remark 5.6 in [26] the metric in the double null gauge (U𝒞​ℋ2+,V𝒞​ℋ1+)(U_{\mathcal{CH}_{2}^{+}},V_{\mathcal{CH}_{1}^{+}}) extends continuously to the bifurcate Cauchy horizon {V𝒞​ℋ1+=1}∪{U𝒞​ℋ2+=1}\{V_{\mathcal{CH}_{1}^{+}}=1\}\cup\{U_{\mathcal{CH}_{2}^{+}}=1\}, where we have used the notation from [26]. Moreover, (5.19) in [26] then implies that limV𝒞​ℋ1+→1∂V𝒞​ℋ1+r=−∞\lim\limits_{V_{\mathcal{CH}_{1}^{+}}\to 1}\partial_{V_{\mathcal{CH}_{1}^{+}}}r=-\infty, and similarly for the left Cauchy horizon. The statement that ∂U𝒞​ℋ2+r<0\partial_{U_{\mathcal{CH}_{2}^{+}}}r<0 near the right Cauchy horizon follows trivially from the Raychaudhuri equation (2.4) in [26] and the fact that ∂U𝒞​ℋ2+r<0\partial_{U_{\mathcal{CH}_{2}^{+}}}r<0 on the initial data hypersurface in the right exterior. Similarly for the left Cauchy horizon. Thus the assumptions of Theorem 4.3 are met (after a trivial reparametrisation of the null coordinates). ∎

In order to prove the C2C^{2}-formulation of strong cosmic censorship for DLO spacetimes, i.e., their generic C2C^{2}-inextendibility, Luk and Oh use the C2C^{2}-regularity of an assumed extension to infer that there is a radial null geodesic which leaves the DLO spacetime and enters the extension. They then proceed by showing that if the null geodesic approached the Cauchy horizon then the Ricci-curvature contracted twice with the affine velocity vector of this null geodesic would blow up along the null geodesic – and if the null geodesic approached null infinity or i+i^{+}, then rr would go to infinity along the null geodesic or the null geodesic would be affine complete. All of these are contradictions to the assumption that the radial null geodesic enters a C2C^{2}-extension.

The following theorem improves the C2C^{2}-formulation of strong cosmic censorship for DLO spacetimes proven by Luk and Oh to a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-formulation.

Theorem 4.31.

Consider a sufficiently small spherically symmetric perturbation of asymptotically flat two-ended subextremal RN initial data for the Einstein-Maxwell-scalar field system such that the future development is given by Figure 12. Assume the initial data is generic and small in the sense of [27]. Then the future development is future Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible.

Let us remark that we follow here the setting of [27] and only establish the generic future inextendibility of the physically more interesting future development. One would expect3131 31 Private communication with J. Luk. that with a bit more work one can extend [27] to also show that the past Cauchy horizon of the past development becomes singular generically. The time-dual statement of Theorem 4.31 would then also yield the generic past Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility – and thus the generic Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility of the whole spacetime, cf. Lemma 2.5.

Note that Theorem 4.31 goes beyond Theorem 4.30 by the statement that also the black hole exterior is future Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible. The methods used by Luk and Oh for proving the future C2C^{2}-inextendibility of the exterior do not transfer to locally Lipschitz regularity. Theorem A.2 together with Proposition A.14 in the appendix show however that the estimates obtained by Luk and Oh in [27] can be used to establish the timelike geodesic completeness of the exterior in the sense of Theorem A.2, which we can then use as an obstruction to Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extensions of the exterior.

Proof.

The proof is by contradiction, so let ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} be a future Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension and let p~∈∂+ι⁡(M)\tilde{p}\in\partial^{+}\iota(M), where (M,g)(M,g) denotes the generic DLO spacetime under consideration. By Proposition 2.6 there exists a chart φ~:U~→(−ε0,ε0)×(−ε1,ε1)d=:Rε0,ε1\tilde{\varphi}:\tilde{U}\to(-\varepsilon_{0},\varepsilon_{0})\times(-\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{1})^{d}=:R_{\varepsilon_{0},\varepsilon_{1}} as in Proposition 2.6 with δ>0\delta>0 so small that all vectors in C5/6+C^{+}_{\nicefrac{{5}}{{6}}} are future directed timelike, all vectors in C5/6−C^{-}_{\nicefrac{{5}}{{6}}} are past directed timelike, and all vectors in C5/8cC^{c}_{\nicefrac{{5}}{{8}}} are spacelike. By Proposition 2.11 there exists a future directed timelike geodesic γ:[−μ,0)→M\gamma:[-\mu,0)\to M that is future inextendible in MM and such that φ~∘ι∘γ:[−μ,0)→Rε0,ε1\tilde{\varphi}\circ\iota\circ\gamma:[-\mu,0)\to R_{\varepsilon_{0},\varepsilon_{1}} maps below the graph of ff and has a future endpoint on the graph of ff. We also define γ~:=ι∘γ\tilde{\gamma}:=\iota\circ\gamma.

If there exists a point on γ\gamma that lies on the event horizons or in the interior, then we clearly have that γ\gamma approaches to the future the bifurcate Cauchy horizon. Then the restriction of ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} to the black hole interior gives rise in particular to a future Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension of the black hole interior3232 32 Take a future directed smooth timelike curve of constant x0x_{0} in the chart φ~\tilde{\varphi} starting at a point of γ~\tilde{\gamma} which is contained in the black hole interior. This curve then intersects the graph of ff in, as a result by definition, a future boundary point of the interior., which is a contradiction to Theorem 4.30.

If γ\gamma starts in one of the black hole exteriors then by Proposition A.14 γ\gamma is future complete or crosses the event horizon. We have already ruled out that it can cross the event horizon, so it must be future complete. We then reparametrise γ~\tilde{\gamma} by the x0x_{0}-coordinate in the chart φ~\tilde{\varphi} to obtain a curve which we denote again by γ~:[s0,s1)→U~⊆M~\tilde{\gamma}:[s_{0},s_{1})\to\tilde{U}\subseteq\tilde{M}, with −ε0<s0<s1<ε0-\varepsilon_{0}<s_{0}<s_{1}<\varepsilon_{0}. Using the uniform bound |g~μ​ν−mμ​ν|<δ|\tilde{g}_{\mu\nu}-m_{\mu\nu}|<\delta and (2.10) we compute

∫s0s1−g~​(γ~˙​(s),γ~˙​(s)CLOSE​𝑑s≤2​ε0⋅C⁡(δ,‖γ~˙‖ℝ4)<∞,\int_{s_{0}}^{s_{1}}\sqrt{-\tilde{g}(\dot{\tilde{\gamma}}(s),\dot{\tilde{\gamma}}(s)}\,ds\leq 2\varepsilon_{0}\cdot C(\delta,||\dot{\tilde{\gamma}}||_{\mathbb{R}^{4}})<\infty\;,

which is a contradiction to the future completeness of γ\gamma. Thus (M,g)(M,g) is future Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible. ∎

Appendix A Timelike geodesic completeness of the exterior of spherically symmetric black holes

Here we present a very general criterion for the exterior of a spherically symmetric black hole spacetime to be future timelike geodesically complete in the sense that any future directed and future inextendible timelike geodesic that starts in the exterior is future complete or enters the black hole region. This result is in particular needed to prove the future Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility of the Dafermos-Luk-Oh (DLO) spacetimes in Theorem 4.31. Note that the timelike geodesic completeness of the exterior of the DLO spacetimes does not seem to follow directly from [27] since the weak stability estimates in Theorem 8.6, in particular (8.37), degenerate near the horizon and do not give asymptotic stability. Thus, a perturbative argument, deducing the geodesic completeness of the exterior of the DLO spacetimes from the geodesic completeness of the exterior of a subextremal Reissner-Nordström solution, seems to fail. We circumvent this obstacle by changing from the double null coordinates used in [27] to (v,r)(v,r)-coordinates, in which the weak stability estimates give orbital stability. Supplemented by a few further conditions in the exterior, see (A.15) - (A.19), which can be verified directly from the estimates obtained in [27], this suffices to infer the geodesic completeness of the exterior.

We consider a general spherically symmetric spacetime (M,g)(M,g) in (v,r)(v,r)-coordinates, where

M=[0,∞)×(0,∞)⏟=:Q×𝕊2M=\underbrace{[0,\infty)\times(0,\infty)}_{=:Q}\times\mathbb{S}^{2}

with standard (v,r)(v,r)-coordinates on the first two factors and

(A.1) g=−f⁡(v,r)​d​v2+h⁡(v,r)2​(d​v⊗d​r+d​r⊗d​v)+r2​γ̊,g=-f(v,r)\,dv^{2}+\frac{h(v,r)}{2}\,\big(dv\otimes dr+dr\otimes dv\big)+r^{2}\,\mathring{\gamma}\;,

    v˙​(s)≤h⁡(sn)h⁡(s)​[∫sns2​L2h⁡(sn)​r3​(s′)​d​s′+v˙​(sn)]≤C[C⋅|s−sn|+v˙(sn)] for all sn≤s<b.\begin{split}\dot{v}(s)&\leq\frac{h(s_{n})}{h(s)}\Big[\int\limits_{s_{n}}^{s}\frac{2L^{2}}{h(s_{n})r^{3}(s^{\prime})}\,ds^{\prime}+\dot{v}(s_{n})\Big]\\ &\leq C\big[C\cdot|s-s_{n}|+\dot{v}(s_{n})\big]\qquad\textnormal{ for all }s_{n}\leq s<b\;.\end{split}

    Given ε>0\varepsilon>0 we can now choose nn large enough such that 0<v˙​(s)<ε0<\dot{v}(s)<\varepsilon for all sn<s<bs_{n}<s<b.

    It now follows from (A.10) together with (A.3) that r˙​(s)→−∞\dot{r}(s)\to-\infty for s→bs\to b, which, together with r>cℋ+r>c_{\mathcal{H}^{+}} along γ\gamma, implies that lims→br⁡(s)∈[cℋ+,∞)\lim_{s\to b}r(s)\in[c_{\mathcal{H}^{+}},\infty) exists. This concludes the proof.

∎

Let now (M,g)(M,g) be a spherically symmetric spacetime in double null coordinates (u,v)(u,v), i.e., let

M=ℝ×[0,∞)⏟=:Q×𝕊2M=\underbrace{\mathbb{R}\times[0,\infty)}_{=:Q}\times\mathbb{S}^{2}

with canonical (u,v)(u,v)-coordinates on the first two factors and

g=−Ω22​(d​u⊗d​v+d​v⊗d​u)+r2​γ̊,g=-\frac{\Omega^{2}}{2}\big(du\otimes dv+dv\otimes du\big)+r^{2}\,\mathring{\gamma}\;,

where Ω:Q→(0,∞)\Omega:Q\to(0,\infty) and r:Q→(0,∞)r:Q\to(0,\infty) are smooth functions. We have d​r=∂ur⋅d​u+∂vr⋅d​vdr=\partial_{u}r\cdot du+\partial_{v}r\cdot dv. Assuming that ∂ur\partial_{u}r vanishes nowhere we can globally transform into (v,r)(v,r)-coordinates: we obtain

d​u=d​r−∂vr⋅d​v∂urdu=\frac{dr-\partial_{v}r\cdot dv}{\partial_{u}r}

and thus

g=Ω2​∂vr∂ur​d​v2−Ω22​∂ur​(d​v⊗d​r+d​r⊗d​v)+r2​γ̊.g=\frac{\Omega^{2}\partial_{v}r}{\partial_{u}r}\,dv^{2}-\frac{\Omega^{2}}{2\partial_{u}r}\,\big(dv\otimes dr+dr\otimes dv\big)+r^{2}\,\mathring{\gamma}\;.

Recalling the definition of the Hawking mass m:Q→ℝm:Q\to\mathbb{R} by 1−2​mr:=g−1(dr,dr)=−4Ω2∂ur⋅∂vr1-\frac{2m}{r}:=g^{-1}(dr,dr)=-\frac{4}{\Omega^{2}}\partial_{u}r\cdot\partial_{v}r, introducing the definition κ:=∂vr1−2​mr=−Ω24​∂ur\kappa:=\frac{\partial_{v}r}{1-\frac{2m}{r}}=-\frac{\Omega^{2}}{4\partial_{u}r} and comparing with (A.1) gives

(A.11) f=4​κ⋅∂vr and h=4​κ.f=4\kappa\cdot\partial_{v}r\qquad\textnormal{ and }\qquad h=4\kappa\;.

We moreover note that

∂∂u|v=∂r∂u|v​∂∂r|v.\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\Big|_{v}=\frac{\partial r}{\partial u}\Big|_{v}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\Big|_{v}\;.

Thus we obtain

(A.12) ∂∂r|v​h=4∂ur​∂uκ\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\Big|_{v}h=\frac{4}{\partial_{u}r}\partial_{u}\kappa

and

(A.13) f⋅∂rh−∂rf⋅h=16​κ∂ur(∂vr⋅∂uκ−∂u(κ∂vr))=−16​κ2∂ur⋅∂u∂vr.f\cdot\partial_{r}h-\partial_{r}f\cdot h=\frac{16\kappa}{\partial_{u}r}\big(\partial_{v}r\cdot\partial_{u}\kappa-\partial_{u}(\kappa\partial_{v}r)\big)=-\frac{16\kappa^{2}}{\partial_{u}r}\cdot\partial_{u}\partial_{v}r\;.
Proposition A.14.

Consider a Cauchy hypersurface of a two-ended subextremal Reissner-Nordström black hole and a sufficiently small spherically symmetric perturbation of the Cauchy data under the Einstein-Maxwell-scalar field system as in [27]. Consider one of the exteriors of the arising future development and let (u,v)∈𝒟⊆ℝ×[1,∞)(u,v)\in\mathcal{D}\subseteq\mathbb{R}\times[1,\infty) be null coordinates normalised as in Theorem 8.6 of [27] covering the exterior under consideration. We then have

(A.15) 0<c≤κ≤C\displaystyle 0<c\leq\kappa\leq C
(A.16) 0<∂vr≤C\displaystyle 0<\partial_{v}r\leq C
(A.17) ∂ur<0\displaystyle\partial_{u}r<0
(A.18) ∂uκ≤0\displaystyle\partial_{u}\kappa\leq 0
(A.19) ∂u∂vr≤0\displaystyle\partial_{u}\partial_{v}r\leq 0

in the exterior. In particular it then follows from Theorem A.2 that a future directed future inextendible timelike geodesic starting in the exterior is future complete or crosses the event horizon.

Proof.

(A.15) is directly given by (8.35) or (8.44) in [27]. The positivity of ∂vr\partial_{v}r follows since the exterior is non-trapped and the upper bound in (A.16) follows from (8.46) by comparison with an exact subextremal Reissner-Nordström black hole. The condition (A.17) follows from the Raychauduri equation (2.5) in [27] and it being satisfied along the initial data hypersurface. To show (A.18) we recall that −∂uκκ2=∂uκ−1=4​r​(∂uϕ)2Ω2≥0-\frac{\partial_{u}\kappa}{\kappa^{2}}=\partial_{u}\kappa^{-1}=\frac{4r(\partial_{u}\phi)^{2}}{\Omega^{2}}\geq 0 by the definition κ=−Ω24​∂ur\kappa=-\frac{\Omega^{2}}{4\partial_{u}r} of κ\kappa and the Raychauduri equation (2.5) in [27]. Finally by (2.8) in [27] we have

∂u∂vr=2​(ϖ−e2r)⋅∂ur⋅∂vrr2⋅(1−2​mr)\partial_{u}\partial_{v}r=\frac{2(\varpi-\frac{e^{2}}{r})\cdot\partial_{u}r\cdot\partial_{v}r}{r^{2}\cdot(1-\frac{2m}{r})}

where ϖ=m+e22​r\varpi=m+\frac{e^{2}}{2r} and ee is the charge of the black hole, see [27]. Since ∂vr>0\partial_{v}r>0 in the exterior and by (A.17) we also have 1−2​mr>01-\frac{2m}{r}>0 in the exterior by definition of the Hawking mass mm. In order to show (A.19) it thus suffices to show ϖ−e2r≥0\varpi-\frac{e^{2}}{r}\geq 0 in the exterior, which is equivalent to ϖ⋅r≥e2\varpi\cdot r\geq e^{2}. Note that this is trivially satisfied for rr sufficiently large by (8.43) in [27]. For rr bounded away from ∞\infty we have |r−r¯|≤C​ε|r-\overline{r}|\leq C\varepsilon by (8.45) in [27], where we choose the overlined quantities to denote quantities in an exact subextremal Reissner-Nordström black hole. Using also (8.43) in [27] and the same trivial statement for the charges ee, e¯\overline{e}, which are non-dynamic, we compute for rr bounded away from infinity

ϖ⋅r≥ϖ¯⋅r¯−C​ε≥ϖ¯⋅r¯+−C​ε=ϖ¯​(ϖ¯+ϖ¯2−e¯2)−C​ε>e¯2+ϖ¯​ϖ¯2−e¯2−C​ε≥e2+ϖ¯​ϖ¯2−e¯2−2​C​ε≥e2\begin{split}\varpi\cdot r&\geq\overline{\varpi}\cdot\overline{r}-C\varepsilon\\ &\geq\overline{\varpi}\cdot\overline{r}_{+}-C\varepsilon\\ &=\overline{\varpi}(\overline{\varpi}+\sqrt{\overline{\varpi}^{2}-\overline{e}^{2}})-C\varepsilon\\ &>\overline{e}^{2}+\overline{\varpi}\sqrt{\overline{\varpi}^{2}-\overline{e}^{2}}-C\varepsilon\\ &\geq e^{2}+\overline{\varpi}\sqrt{\overline{\varpi}^{2}-\overline{e}^{2}}-2C\varepsilon\\ &\geq e^{2}\end{split}

for ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small.

Since we have ∂ur<0\partial_{u}r<0 we can now go over to (v,r)(v,r)-coordinates and extend the metric arbitrarily to the full domain [1,∞)×(0,∞)×𝕊2[1,\infty)\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb{S}^{2}. For the curve σℋ+\sigma_{\mathcal{H}^{+}} in Theorem A.2 we choose the event horizon and by (A.11), (A.12), and (A.13) the conditions (A.3) are satisfied in the exterior to the future of any point in the exterior, see also Remark A.4. It thus follows that any future directed future inextendible timelike geodesic starting in the exterior is future complete or crosses the event horizon. ∎
